effective_architecture.rule: Every engine and table claim in the summary must match effective_architecture: name a table under an engine only if that table is in the engine's tables list (the tables its assigned in-scope queries touch), never present an eliminated engine as part of the target, and do not generalise a table to an engine that merely shares a query group with it. deterministic_summary:
Recommendation: move the discourse PostgreSQL database to four AWS services in three waves. Wave 1 moves it to Aurora PostgreSQL, which ends up serving 48.1% of the queries; wave 2 puts ElastiCache in front of 3 hot reads (25.1% of calls); wave 3 moves 42.0% of the queries to DynamoDB and 9.9% to DocumentDB. The projected cost of the full modernization is $536 per month at AWS Price List on-demand prices for us-east-1, retrieved 2026-11-04. No current cost was collected for the source database, so the plan claims no saving against it.

Risk: overall risk is medium. The main exposures are a medium-severity operational risk risk on DynamoDB and a medium-severity operational risk risk on DynamoDB: review them in the risk register before wave 3 starts.

Decision: approve wave 1. It is safe to approve: it moves the database 1:1 to Aurora PostgreSQL, the same engine family as PostgreSQL, with its current data model, and its cutover waits until schema and data parity is validated against the source.

assumptions: On-demand capacity mode for all target databases
Does not include data transfer, backups, or global tables
Reads the cache layer fronts are also billed on their owner engines, as if every one missed the cache (conservative)
39 source tables no in-scope query reads (<0.01 GB) are stored on Aurora PostgreSQL, where wave 1 moves them

The DynamoDB figure includes $0.52/mo for the design's 58 global secondary indexes at on-demand prices: $0.00 of storage (each index's item count times its projected item size plus 100 bytes of index overhead per item) and $0.52 of index writes (one for each put or delete whose item may set the index's keys, two for an update that changes an index key or does not say what it changes, one for an update that changes only a projected attribute, billed at the standard rate per 1 KB of the projected item, on average load with the collected rows per call, an average of exactly zero counted as one row). Index reads are not added, since each is one of its query's reads and already priced, and the free tier is left out
DynamoDB reads are priced eventually consistent, except transactions, which are priced at transactional rates.

risks.description: [dynamodb] trigger: category_settings_require_reply_approval_readonly needs application-side logic on DynamoDB.
risks.mitigation: Implement as application logic: The source trigger raises an error on any insert or update that touches require_reply_approval. The application rejects writes to that attribute before it calls PutItem or UpdateItem.

risks.description: [dynamodb] trigger: category_settings_require_topic_approval_readonly needs application-side logic on DynamoDB.
risks.mitigation: Implement as application logic: The source trigger raises an error on any insert or update that touches require_topic_approval. The application rejects writes to that attribute before it calls PutItem or UpdateItem.

risks.description: [dynamodb] trigger: topic_timers_topic_id_readonly needs application-side logic on DynamoDB.
risks.mitigation: Implement as application logic: The trigger raises an error when topic_id is changed. DynamoDB has no triggers: the application writes topic_id once on PutItem and any UpdateItem on a timer leaves it out; an UpdateItem condition expression can also reject a topic_id change.

risks.description: [aurora_postgresql] 1 query uses a leading-wildcard LIKE or a regular expression on Aurora PostgreSQL: SELECT "user_custom_fields".* FROM "user_custom_fields" INNER JOIN user_fields…. Aurora PostgreSQL indexes a leading-wildcard LIKE and a regular expression with a pg_trgm trigram index (GIN or GiST), an extension to create (the PostgreSQL documentation of pg_trgm describes its index support for LIKE, ILIKE, ~ and ~*).
risks.mitigation: Create the pg_trgm extension and a GIN trigram index on the column (CREATE EXTENSION pg_trgm), which serves this LIKE, word searches included; full-text search (to_tsvector) also ranks word matches.

risks.description: Wave 3: 529 queries read 133 tables on an engine that does not own them. 437 of them read a copy of 83 tables that CDC keeps in sync from Aurora PostgreSQL, DocumentDB and DynamoDB across 6 engine pairs, so a read there can miss a recent write. The other 50 tables are written by no captured query, so a one-time copy serves them.
risks.mitigation: Before Wave 3 starts, set up CDC for each engine pair the sources of truth section lists, and send any read that must see its own write to its source of truth; copy the read-only tables once and confirm nothing outside the captured workload writes them. Compare the row counts on both sides. See the Wave 3 gate in the roadmap.

risks.description: Wave 3: 398 queries were decided by less than 5 points, and 102 more were exact ties a routing rule settled: Aurora PostgreSQL keeps 98 close calls and 44 ties over DynamoDB; DocumentDB takes 125 close calls over Aurora PostgreSQL; Aurora PostgreSQL keeps 71 close calls and 32 ties over DocumentDB; DynamoDB takes 63 close calls and 14 ties over DocumentDB; DynamoDB takes 34 close calls over Aurora PostgreSQL; DocumentDB takes 7 close calls and 12 ties over DynamoDB. A small change in the scores moves them.
risks.mitigation: Confirm the engine for these queries in the assignment review before Wave 3 starts, using the close calls section; move any that fit the runner-up better.

risks.mitigation: Review this trade-off with the team that builds Aurora PostgreSQL before Wave 1 starts, and test each one the application depends on.

risks.description: [documentdb] The DocumentDB schema design records 12 trade-offs to review, listed under Migration trade-offs in the engineering report.
risks.mitigation: Review these trade-offs with the team that builds DocumentDB before Wave 3 starts, and test each one the application depends on.
details: Each source table in scope becomes its own collection, with one exception: reviewable_notes is embedded in reviewables as a notes array

Inet and uuid columns become strings, timestamps become dates, and jsonb or json columns become embedded documents. Credentials such as secrets, tokens and password hashes keep their values and should be encrypted at rest and restricted by role
Only indexes that serve an observed query are created. The source secondary indexes that no observed query reads, and the source unique constraints on those columns, are not carried over
Row counts for most tables are assumed (the source reported no count), so document sizes and index sizes rest on the measured table size divided by the declared row width
Set-based writes (the base scheme repoint, the region renames, and the retention deletes) run as updateMany and deleteMany over an index and are not collection scans
Source ids come from sequences. Existing ids are kept as _id values, and new documents need ids generated by the application, as the color scheme insert does
Source triggers and the badge_posts view guard or read tables that stay on other engines. No application logic in this design replaces them
The form template lookup returns only the template id, so it reads the join collection and skips the template collection. The source join also confirmed the template exists

The notes array in reviewables is bounded by the application at 50 entries. The average is 3.33 notes per reviewable (an assumed count), so the document averages 2.2 KB and stays under 18.2 KB at the cap

The retention delete of rejected incoming emails uses a partial index on created_at limited to documents that have a rejection message, so rows with no message must omit the field instead of storing null

The stale API client report uses a correlated lookup (let and pipeline) to find clients with no recently used key, which needs DocumentDB 8.0.2 or later on an instance-based cluster. The child theme join uses a plain equality lookup, which runs on every version

Two reads filter with a not-equal test on status, and the token log retention delete uses a not-in list on action. DocumentDB cannot use an index for negation, so these filters run after the index scan on the other fields

risks.description: [dynamodb] The DynamoDB schema design records 173 trade-offs to review, listed under Migration trade-offs in the engineering report.
risks.mitigation: Review these trade-offs with the team that builds DynamoDB before Wave 3 starts, and test each one the application depends on.
details: A user_options item is 3,300 bytes by the schema (the measured average row is 7,490 bytes), against the 400 KB item limit, so it stays inline in one item
ActionsByType uses the low-cardinality post_action_type_id as partition key for the existence check of query `-4753344182186834428`
All reads of user_stats (queries `-4271916` and `-8871138`) and all single-key lookups are eventually consistent GetItem calls
Badges stay a single table keyed by id (55 items, 882 bytes each); badge name is unique and non-null in the source but no query in this group reads by it
Categories, their category_groups rows and their category_featured_topics rows share one item collection keyed by category_id, with sort keys META, GROUP#group_id#id and FEATURED#topic_id

Child tables are keyed by their parent or lookup column plus the unique partner column, and the source surrogate id stays as a plain attribute: ai_agent_mcp_servers (ai_agent_id, ai_mcp_server_id), category_required_tag_groups (category_id, tag_group_id), group_category_notification_defaults (group_id, category_id), group_tag_notification_defaults (group_id, tag_id), group_mentions (post_id, group_id), theme_site_settings (theme_id, name)
Counts of user_actions (queries `-8883206` and `-2719095`) and reviewables (query `1175638`) are Query calls with Select=COUNT on a GSI keyed by the counted column

Deleting a token by id (query `85658365`) and confirming a token by id (query `-8086318`) look up token_hash in TokenById with a Query, then write the base item. The two id-only writes run at 0.0012 requests per second together, against 0.0006 for the token_hash read, so the id index is the minority path by key rate
Due timers are read from the sparse index DueTimersByType (partition key active_type, sort key execute_at), where active_type is written only while deleted_at is null

Each table is keyed by the column its in-scope queries look up by, so bookmarks, poll_votes, user_badges, quoted_posts, upload_references, topic_views, group_users and do_not_disturb_timings no longer use the source's generated id as their key
Existence checks on reviewable_scores (by score type) and user_badges (by badge and grant time) read KEYS_ONLY indexes, ScoresByType and BadgeGrantsByDate

Filters on non-key columns are applied as FilterExpressions after a Query on the user: user_second_factors (method, enabled; query `763652916241229345`), user_api_keys (attribute_not_exists(revoked_at); query `7661205089442229807`), email_change_requests (change_state not equal; query `-2135502268557629957`) and directory_columns (icon absent; query `1217360975432785261`)

Five GSIs on reviewables and four on user_actions serve the status, topic, target, creator, action type and user-reference lookups, with KEYS_ONLY for the delete and count paths, INCLUDE of latest_score for the score filter, and ALL for the full-row reads

Four tables switch from the generated id to a natural key: translation_overrides (locale, translation_key), plugin_store_rows (plugin_name, key), topic_voting_topic_vote_count (topic_id) and watched_words (action, then id as sort key)
GSI reads are eventually consistent and lag the base item until DynamoDB applies the write to the index
Generated ids move to the application: the source's serial id has no DynamoDB counterpart, so the insert and the copy (INSERT ... SELECT) write an application-generated id
Generated integer ids (categories.id, flags.id, themes.id, invites.id) stay as the item keys, and the application generates ids for new rows
Ids that the source database generated from a sequence are generated by the application
Ids the database generated (search_logs.id, onceoff_logs.id) are generated by the application, and the inserts carry attribute_not_exists(id)

Inserts into schema_migration_details, post_stats and color_scheme_colors (queries `-4917791749421847216`, `5423936073563966392`, `-8362095136812523352`) used database-generated ids; the application now generates the id and each PutItem carries attribute_not_exists(id)

Invites and invited_users form one item collection keyed by invite_id; InvitedUsersByUser (sparse on redeemed_at, keys only) finds a user's redeemed invites and InvitesByEmail (sparse on email, all attributes) finds invites by email, with deleted_at filtered after the read

Item sizes stay inline: the largest is permalinks at 2476 bytes and then sidebar_urls at 1371 bytes, against the 400 KB item limit. Row counts for every table are derived from the table size, because the source has no counts for them
Items stay inline: the table's avg_row_size_bytes is 1405 and the schema item size is 417 bytes, against the 400 KB item limit, and the table has no TEXT or BLOB columns
No in-scope write inserts or changes a unique attribute, so no sentinel items are created
No sentinel items are written for the unique indexes on badge_types.name, watched_words (action, word) and the topic_custom_fields partial unique indexes

No table or index carries load near a partition limit: the highest is post_search_data at about 0.13 RCU/s against 3,000 per key value, and the highest write is upload_references at 0.0229 WCU/s against 1,000
ORDER BY id on the reviewables reads (queries `2643383` and `5026464`) is done by the application, because the GSI sort key is score or created_at
Password reads (query `-8450912255165174963`) are strongly consistent GetItem calls on the base table
PostsById projects ALL attributes because the id reads return the full post (53 attributes) and no in-scope query writes posts

Queries `-5857369` (delete of topic_users by user_id) and `931558391` (update of topic_users notification_level by user_id) write topic_users, which another design group owns, so this group defines no access pattern for them

Query `-5272548625492493566` is served by several requests: a Query on the posts TopicPosts index, a GetItem on topic_users, a GetItem on category_users, and a Query on topic_tags followed by GetItems on tag_users
Query `4582415969089977699`, a UNION of existence probes over post_actions and reviewable_scores, is not given an access pattern (query type OTHER)

Query `5884248130138369695` joins post_replies to posts; DynamoDB serves it as a Query on the RepliesByReplyPost index followed by a BatchGetItem of the posts by id, with the deleted_at IS NULL test applied by the application

Query `7771545769178583636` deletes sidebar_section_links rows by user_id, a table the group 5 design owns. This draft defines a placeholder with the owner's key (PK user_id, SK link_key) so the delete is a Query on the base table plus BatchWriteItem instead of a Scan
Reads by id (`GetItem`, `BatchGetItem`) are eventually consistent and users are updated in place with a condition that the item exists

Reads that return a whole small table in order (all featured topics by rank, all flags by position, all theme ids) use an index whose partition key is the constant ALL, written only on the items each read returns
ReviewablesByStatus, ReviewablesByStatusScore and UserActionsByType have a low-cardinality partition key (status, action_type)

Row counts for ai_agents, api_key_scopes, directory_columns, email_change_requests, embeddable_hosts, screened_ip_addresses, topic_embeds, user_api_keys, user_associated_accounts, user_auth_tokens and user_second_factors are derived from each table's size, because the collector has no count for them. The read rates for these tables are unmeasured peaks (peak factor 1)
Row counts for category_custom_fields (38) and topic_timers (13) are derived from the tables' data size over the item size

Row counts for onceoff_logs, theme_modifier_sets, upcoming_change_events, web_hook_event_types and web_hook_event_types_hooks are derived from each table's size, because the source has no count for them. search_logs.user_agent (declared up to 2000 bytes, counted at 1 KB in the item size) stays inline: the table's average row is 195 bytes against the 400 KB item limit
Row counts for optimized_images (33) and uploads (9) are derived from the tables' data size over the item size
Row counts for post_replies and topic_tags are not collected, so their item counts are 0 in this draft
Rows with a NULL user_id in poll_votes (nullable in the source) cannot be keyed by user_id; topic_views uses the viewer key USER#id, or IP#address when user_id is NULL
SELECT DISTINCT user_id over dismissed_topic_users (query `8521344751852874806`) is served by the sparse GSI DismissedUsers, keyed on a constant marker that only dismissed items carry
Tag names, tag slugs and tag group names are copied onto the category_tag_links items so the category tag lists need one Query and no join

Telemetry reports 0 returned rows for most key lookups, and row counts are assumed for category_users, dismissed_topic_users, discourse_solved_solved_topics and user_visits; the design prices each key lookup at one item and treats existence checks as returning none

The GSIs AssociatedAccountsByProviderUser (provider_name, user_id), TopicEmbedsByTopic (topic_id), DirectoryColumnsByName (name, type) and ScreenedIpByActionType (action_type, last_activity_at) serve queries `-7832492340302674463`, `2931539718557711172`, `1217360975432785261` and `-5195588254230218940`. The first, third and fourth project all attributes because their reads return the whole item; TopicEmbedsByTopic projects only deleted_at for its filter

The IN list of topic ids in the PAT-6 reads becomes a BatchGetItem of up to 100 (topic_id, user_id) keys, and the notification_level and notifications_reason_id predicates of queries `-3292419205471075412` and `-6617783115228636850` are evaluated by the application on the item returned by GetItem
The IN-list reads on post_custom_fields and category_custom_fields (up to 7 names and up to 7 categories by 10 names) become a Query per partition key with a name filter expression

The INSERT ... SELECT copy on web_hook_event_types_hooks (query `2584108843483812003`) is a Query on the partition web_hook_event_type_id followed by a BatchWriteItem under the target type id; the table is keyed by (web_hook_event_type_id, web_hook_id), the source's unique pair

The IS NOT NULL and equality filters on theme_modifier_sets (queries `-1911262412598852204` and `5076669123351474512`) are evaluated by the application on the GetItem result, since a NULL column has no attribute on the item
The ThemeFieldsById index (KEYS_ONLY) maps a theme field's id to its table key for the value_baked update

The UPDATE of query `6213645647369225488` that appends text to details cannot run as one statement; it becomes a Query on the ActorActions GSI (acting_user_id, projecting details) with an action filter, then one conditional UpdateItem per record
The admin_notices delete by subject and identifier is served by a NoticesBySubjectIdentifier GSI keyed on both columns, projecting details
The categories table has avg_row_size_bytes of 20972 against a schema item size of 3088; description and topic_template stay inline as text attributes

The category notification lookup of query `4253263512682689512` joins topics through a subquery; the application reads the topic's category_id from the topics owner's item and then issues a GetItem on the category row
The category_posting_review_groups lookup (query `-7096413`) is keyed on category_id with a sort key of post_type#group_id, and the IN list of 8 categories becomes 8 Queries
The category_required_tag_groups read ordered by the order column is a Query on the category_id partition; the application sorts the items by the order attribute

The consistency repair sweep (query `2539559289466738950`) that clears granted_title_badge_id where the user's title is empty is modeled at write time: the write path that changes a user's title issues a conditional UpdateItem on that user's profile. users is owned by another design group, which designs its writes; this group defines no write to users
The content column stays inline: the table's average row is 75,215 bytes against the 400 KB item limit, and 52 rows total 3.73 MB

The cross-user update of a custom field value (query `2866689475356927595`) is a Query on CustomFieldsByNameValue (partition key name and value) followed by an UpdateItem per item. The value column is text and a key attribute holds at most 2048 bytes for a partition key
The database generated the id of uploads, optimized_images and sidebar_section_links; the application now generates these ids before the write

The deleted_at IS NULL and post_type IN (...) conditions run as FilterExpressions (GetItem and BatchGetItem results are checked by the application), and the sort_order ordering is applied by the application
The do-not-disturb check is a Query on user_id with the sort key (starts_at plus id) at or below now, then a filter on ends_at above now

The duplicate clean-up (query `-2784383`), the consistency repair of target_topic_id (query `-8208700`) and the delete by any of three user references (query `3015126`) are modeled by their target-native approach, not as a Scan plus batch write
The embeddings column (halfvec) is stored as a binary attribute and the 19-row tables carry no vector search query in this group
The filter on last_read_post_number in query `-2081487299388086276` is a FilterExpression on the Query of one topic's partition

The five set-based deletes by a key column (given_daily_likes, poll_votes and topic_views by user, quoted_posts by post, upload_references by target) are served as a Query on the partition key followed by BatchWriteItem deletes in batches of 25
The full read of badges.icon (query `-5609072216516021935`) is a Query on the BadgesAll index, whose partition key is the constant 'all'
The id column was generated by a database sequence; the application now generates it and writes it as an attribute
The id columns of users and theme_fields were generated by the database (sequences, returned by INSERT ... RETURNING); the application now generates them
The id of javascript_caches was generated by the database and is now generated by the application, because the item key JSCACHE#{id} must exist before the transaction is sent
The id values that the source database generated for topic_users and topic_tags are generated by the application
The id-based update (query `-1896810`) first queries SettingsById for the name, then runs UpdateItem on that name
The llm_models listing (query `-7865273`) has no filter, so it is served by a GSI whose partition key is the constant attribute catalog and whose sort key is id

The newest-ids read and the delete of older ids for one target use the GSI StylesheetsByTargetAndId (target, id) with a KEYS_ONLY projection; the delete queries the index and then removes items by table key with BatchWriteItem
The optimized_images update by id (query `-929154033288984175`) addresses the item by upload_id and variant, taken from the loaded record; no index on the surrogate id exists

The orphan clean-up of topic_search_data (query `-1857846`) is modeled as a DynamoDB Streams consumer on the topics table that deletes the search item by topic_id, in place of the source's join-and-delete sweep

The query `-5195588254230218940` tests last_match_at < cutoff OR (last_match_at IS NULL AND created_at < cutoff); the design stores last_activity_at (last_match_at, or created_at when never matched) as the GSI sort key and reads it with one range condition. action_type has few distinct values and the table 50 items
The query `3689045540` that expires a user's other tokens runs as a Query on the TokensByUser index (partition key user_id) with a filter on scope and id, followed by one UpdateItem per returned item

The query `5571699630796892942` reads every embeddable host with no filter; the design stores all 22 items under the constant partition key embeddable_scope = ALL and reads them with one Query instead of a Scan. The query returned 0 rows on average in the collector, so 22 items (the table's row count) are used for sizing
The retention delete (query `-6072012279523579697`) is served by Time to Live on an expires_at epoch attribute set to created_at plus the retention period, not by a Scan and batch delete

The retention deletes on search_logs (query `3022359024859565856`) and unsubscribe_keys (query `9113575919552827162`) become Time to Live on an expires_at epoch attribute, written as created_at plus the retention period on every insert
The reviewable_histories delete by created_by_id is served by a keys-only HistoryByCreator GSI followed by BatchWriteItem deletes of up to 25 items per call
The reviewables payload JSON column is stored as a map attribute, and the reviewables row count of 9 is derived from the table size of 0.08 MB over the item size
The scheduler_stats retention delete `5139002051034385017` is served by Time to Live on an expires_at epoch-seconds attribute (started_at plus the retention period) set at insert
The security-key existence check of query `5146492642468846180` is a Query on the factor-type prefix with a filter on enabled and a limit of one item
The shared_drafts IN-list reads (nine statements, pattern PAT-8) become BatchGetItem on topic_id; the source lists up to 36 ids per statement
The skipped_email_logs retention delete (query `-5145007`) becomes Time to Live on an expires_at epoch attribute written with each log item
The source generates ids for user_histories rows (RETURNING id) and the other tables; the application generates the id of each new user_histories item before PutItem
The source has no row count for allowed_pm_users, anonymous_users, shared_drafts, tag_users, drafts and polls, so their item_count values come from the table sizes in design_metrics
The source tables carry no tenant column, so partition keys do not lead with a tenant attribute

The source unique indexes on (category_id, user_id), (user_id, visited_at), (user_id, draft_key), (user_id, topic_id) and user_options.user_id are enforced by the table primary key (user_id plus sort key), and user_options inserts carry `attribute_not_exists(user_id)`

The source unique indexes on groups (name, incoming_email), tags (name) and category_settings (category_id) get no sentinel items; category_settings is keyed by category_id, so the key itself enforces it

The source's retention delete (query `-805676`) of unconfirmed, expired tokens past a cut-off becomes Time to Live on expires_at_epoch, written as created_at in epoch seconds plus the retention period only while confirmed is false and expired is true
The table is keyed by the natural unique key (target, digest) instead of the surrogate id; the id stays as an attribute and is generated by the application

The table is keyed on the setting name instead of the source id: the name is unique and NOT NULL (unique index index_site_settings_on_name), 27 distinct values over 27 rows, and 6 of 9 patterns look rows up by name

The table is keyed on token_hash instead of the source's surrogate id, because token_hash is unique and not null in the source, stable, evenly distributed (97 distinct values in 97 rows) and the key of the token confirmation lookup

The tag_users and topic_tags subquery (query `-5481939`) is split: the application reads the tag ids of the topic from the owner of topic_tags, then calls BatchGetItem on tag_users for those keys, filters levels 3 and 4 and sorts them descending
The text columns (topic_custom_fields.value, plugin_store_rows.value, skipped_email_logs.custom_reason, translation_overrides.original_translation) stay inline in their items
The text columns raw, cooked and raw_email stay inline in the post item
The theme lookup (query `24832854`) reads the sparse JavascriptCacheByTheme index keyed on theme_id with ALL projection; only records with a theme_id are indexed
The theme_site_settings read with two theme ids becomes two parallel Query calls, one per theme_id, and the sidebar_urls read of 12 ids becomes one BatchGetItem

The three DELETE statements by model_id (queries `-1435330` `524039068` `499176814` as embeddings cleanups) are served by keying each embeddings table on model_id with a composite sort key of strategy and entity id

The topic reads by id use BatchGetItem for the IN list (7.5 ids on average, at most 100 per call) and GetItem for single ids. The deleted_at IS NULL and archetype conditions are evaluated by the application on the returned item, because a deleted_at attribute is absent when null
The topics placeholder serves two GetItem reads (queries `6746886374591153495`, `6004114026531250967`); the deleted_at IS NULL filter becomes an application check on the item
The tracker row averages 4033 bytes (details JSON), under the 400 KB item limit, and stays inline as a map attribute
The tsvector column search_data of post_search_data is not migrated; the DynamoDB item keeps raw_data, locale, version and private_message
The tsvector columns search_data of topic_search_data and user_search_data are not stored; only raw_data, locale and version are written by the upserts (queries `34182582` and `76836928`)
The two UPDATE statements on users (`2150880814507944816` and `8321624443266976557`) are served at write time, not as set-based sweeps
The unfiltered read of all settings (query `-5236333`, no WHERE) becomes a Query on AllSettings, whose partition key is the constant attribute scope = SITE, holding all 27 rows, instead of a Scan
The unique constraint on user_actions is enforced by the primary key itself with attribute_not_exists(action_key) on the PutItem, so no sentinel item is written
The unique index on (user_id, primary) of user_emails is enforced with a sentinel item UNIQ#PRIMARY#<primary> in the user's partition, written in the same TransactWriteItems as the email
The unique indexes on post_custom_fields.post_id and topic_timers.timerable_id and topic_id are not enforced with sentinel items; both tables are keyed with the generated id as sort key
The upload url query adds conditions on created_at and retain_hours and an id cursor. The index Query keys on url and the id range; the retention and cutoff conditions run as a FilterExpression

The user-scoped tables category_users, dismissed_topic_users, draft_sequences, user_options, user_security_keys and user_visits share one item collection, `user_data`, keyed by user_id with a typed sort key

The user_fields full scan (query `-2453444`) becomes a Query on one item collection with the constant partition key field_scope, and the position-ordered read (query `3003621`) sorts its 14 items in the application
The users table keeps the source id as its key (`user_id`) and serves the lookup by lower-cased username through the UsersByUsernameLower index

The visibility check joins category_groups to group_users for the caller's groups. The category and its group rows come from one Query on categories; the caller's group ids come from the owner group's design of group_users, and the application intersects the two sets
The visit count of query `-5378124675010793632` is a Query with Select=COUNT on the user's visit range (SK greater than the date) with a filter on posts_read

The whole-table reads of custom_emojis (ordered by name), site_setting_groups and topic_voting_category_settings use a constant partition attribute (emoji_scope, setting_scope, voting_scope) with the name or category_id as sort key, so they are Queries and never Scans

Three GSIs are added: TokensByEmail (email), TokensByUser (user_id, email) and TokenById (id). The first two project all attributes because their reads return the full item; TokenById projects keys only because it only finds the token_hash for a write. Updates of expired and confirmed do not change any index key

Three global secondary indexes serve lookups the base keys cannot: UploadsByUrl (url, upload_id range), UploadsBySha1 (sha1) and SidebarLinksBySection (linkable_type and sidebar_section_id, position order). All project ALL because the reads return the whole item
Topics, uploads and user profiles keep the source surrogate id as the table key. topics.external_id and uploads.sha1 are unique but nullable, so they are not keys

Unique usernames and secure identifiers are enforced with sentinel items in the user_unique_values table, written in the same TransactWriteItems as the user, each Put guarded by attribute_not_exists(unique_value)
UserEmailsById is a sparse-free INCLUDE index on email_id that serves the delete by id (query `-7887291093737212990`)

Wide columns stay inline: groups averages 8156 bytes per row and api_keys 73400 bytes, against the 400 KB item limit; the row counts of bookmarks, category_settings, reviewable_scores, tags, topic_views and upload_references are derived from the table size

ai_agents has a unique name that the insert `7964039920894090174` sets, so the insert writes the agent and a name sentinel item in one TransactWriteItems call, each Put guarded by attribute_not_exists(ai_agent_key)

ai_agents rows average 3755 bytes (system_prompt is declared up to 10,000,000 characters), far below the 400 KB item limit, so system_prompt, description and tools stay inline. The table has 36 rows, derived from the table's size
ai_agents stays keyed by the surrogate id (AGENT#id) because the read `-9107418073878310695` looks agents up by id; name is unique and not null but no in-scope read uses it
allowed_pm_users copies the username of the allowed user from users into each item, replacing the join in query `-4829209`
anonymous_users is keyed on master_user_id, which has a unique index over a non-null column, and the active = true condition of query `11714267` is checked on the returned item

application_requests is keyed by its unique natural key (date, req_type) and web_crawler_requests by (date, user_agent); the generated id stays as a plain attribute. Both tables are small counters read and written by that key only. The upsert `6668674146221133871` becomes an UpdateItem with ADD count
backup_metadata ids come from a PostgreSQL sequence in the source and are generated by the application in DynamoDB; the insert carries attribute_not_exists(id)
badge_types and color_schemes keep the generated id as partition key
category_custom_fields gets the index CategoryFieldsByName (partition key name, sort key value, keys only) for the lookup of categories by field name and value
discourse_solved_solved_topics is keyed on topic_id instead of the surrogate id, because every read looks a topic up by it and the source holds a unique index on topic_id over a NOT NULL column

drafts is keyed on the natural pair user_id and draft_key instead of the generated id, because the source has a unique index on (user_id, draft_key) over non-null columns and every read and the delete by user (query `33950506`) address it
external_upload_stubs gets a GSI on status (partition) and created_at (sort) for the retention delete (query `11537686`), which is a status plus time-range filter with no key value
group_requests and reviewable_claimed_topics deletes by user_id (queries `45187686` and `60515295`) run as a Query on a KEYS_ONLY GSI keyed on user_id plus BatchWriteItem deletes

javascript_caches is an item collection with sentinel items for the unique theme_id and the unique (theme_field_id, name) pair, which the insert (query `79675277`) writes with the record in one TransactWriteItems of at most 3 items, each Put guarded by attribute_not_exists(cache_key). The record is keyed by the application-generated id

muted_users becomes its own table keyed by user_id and muted_user_id; the join to users in the muted-users list is dropped because the list returns only the muted user's id, which the key already holds

onceoff_logs gets the OnceoffByJobName index (KEYS_ONLY) for the existence check by job_name (query `1472164085369536536`); job_name is nullable and not unique in the source, so it is not the table key
onceoff_logs keeps a constant partition key onceoff_scope with the generated id as sort key, so the list-all read (query `-7989811519127883198`) is a Query and not a Scan

permalinks, developers and push_subscriptions key on their natural lookup column (url, user_id) instead of the surrogate id; theme_settings, push_subscriptions and post_hotlinked_media use the lookup column as partition key and the id as sort key
polls is keyed on post_id and the poll id as sort key, so both reads by post (queries `-4457441` and `-3763155`) are a Query and the ORDER BY id comes from the sort key
post_actions is keyed by user_id with the action id as sort key, and the user and post lookup runs on the ActionsByUserPost index
post_timings is keyed by topic_id with a composite sort key user_id#post_number, plus the PostTimingsByUser KEYS_ONLY index
posts is keyed by topic_id and post_number instead of the surrogate id, with the PostsById index on id
problem_check_trackers is keyed on the natural pair identifier and target instead of the generated id
reviewable_claimed_topics is keyed on topic_id instead of the surrogate id because topic_id is unique and NOT NULL in the source (one claim per topic)
scheduler_stats keeps the application-generated numeric id as partition key; the source sequence is replaced by an id the application generates
schema_migrations uses a constant partition key (ledger) with version as sort key

sidebar_section_links is keyed by user_id and a link_key of '<linkable_type>#<linkable_id>', the natural unique key (user_id, linkable_type, linkable_id), and optimized_images by upload_id and a variant of '<width>x<height>#<extension>', the natural unique key (upload_id, width, height, extension). Both are unique on the source's evidence (unique indexes on NOT NULL columns) and immutable in the queries

sitemaps is keyed by its unique, non-null name because the read `-8729198876356079750` looks it up by name; the id stays as an attribute. The table has 3 items, and its measured average row size of 17476 bytes comes from page overhead, so the schema size of 178 bytes is used
tag_users has the TagUsersByLevel index on (user_id, notification_level) with KEYS_ONLY projection for the tag id lookup (query `-2955284`)
theme_fields is keyed by theme_id with the sort key field_key = target_id#type_id#name, the source's unique key, so the insert is a PutItem guarded by attribute_not_exists(theme_id)
theme_fields keeps its text columns (value, value_baked) inline

theme_svg_sprites is keyed on theme_id and user_uploads on (user_id, upload_id) because the source unique indexes are NOT NULL and the queries `28794562` and `-29379276` look them up by exactly those columns
topic_custom_fields is keyed by topic_id with the sort key name#id, not by topic_id and name alone
topic_tags is keyed by topic_id and tag_id and has no index on tag_id; the posts placeholder is keyed by id with a TopicPosts index on topic_id and post_number
topic_timers is keyed on the string timerable_key (type and timerable_id) with id as sort key
topic_users is keyed by topic_id (partition) and user_id (sort) instead of the generated id; the source's unique (topic_id, user_id) pair becomes the primary key
upcoming_change_events is keyed by the natural unique pair (event_type, upcoming_change_name), the source's unique index on non-null columns, not by the surrogate id; the id stays as an attribute

uploads.sha1 is unique and the upload insert writes it, so the insert is one TransactWriteItems of 2 items: the upload and a sentinel item in upload_sha1_sentinels, with attribute_not_exists(sha1) on the sentinel Put
user_actions is keyed by user_id with the natural key (action_type, acting_user_id, target_topic_id, target_post_id) as the sort key `action_key`, and the surrogate id stays a plain attribute

user_custom_fields is keyed by user_id with sort key name#id, not by (user_id, name): the source's unique indexes on (name, user_id) are partial indexes for specific names, and the plain (user_id, name) index is not unique
user_emails keeps the surrogate-free key user_id plus EMAIL#id in an item collection rather than keying on the email address
user_histories gets two GSIs, ActorActions (acting_user_id, action) and TargetUserActions (target_user_id, action, created_at), each projecting only the attributes its read uses
user_notification_schedules gets a sparse index EnabledSchedules keyed on enabled_marker, an attribute written only while enabled is true

user_passwords and theme_modifier_sets are keyed by user_id and theme_id, the unique non-null columns their reads use, instead of the surrogate id; the id stays as an attribute. The password delete (query `-5476648005661698537`) addresses the item by user_id with the condition id = :id
user_profiles (avg_row_size_bytes 2572) and uploads (2294) keep their capped text columns (location, website, origin) inline

users is a placeholder owned by group 0, keyed by id, with three indexes this group's queries need: UsersByUsername (ALL), UsersByUsernameLower (KEYS_ONLY) and UsersByUploadedAvatar (KEYS_ONLY, keyed on the nullable uploaded_avatar_id)

risks.description: [elasticache] The ElastiCache schema design records 5 trade-offs to review, listed under Migration trade-offs in the engineering report.
risks.mitigation: Review these trade-offs with the team that builds ElastiCache before Wave 2 starts, and test each one the application depends on.
details: API key rows are cached by key hash with a 60 second TTL, and only keys with revoked_at null are cached
API key scopes are cached as one serialized array per API key, with an empty array cached for a key with no scopes
All three workloads are single-key reads of small values, with an estimated total below 1 MB
The key hash is a credential and forms part of the cache key name
User rows are cached by lowercase username with a 300 second TTL, and the application deletes the key after each owner write

risks.description: [documentdb] Routing assumes a redesign for 1 query on DocumentDB: it scored it with 1 key the source does not have, so the plan holds only if the DocumentDB design adds it. 1 key has no cardinality statistics.
risks.mitigation: Give each of this query the keys routing assumed in the DocumentDB design, check a key with few or unknown distinct values for hot partitions, and serve none of them as a scan. See the Wave 3 gate in the roadmap.
details: A key on themes.color_scheme_id: read as key-scoped 1:N read instead of ad hoc filter.

risks.description: [dynamodb] Routing assumes a redesign for 9 queries on DynamoDB: it scored them with 7 keys the source does not have, so the plan holds only if the DynamoDB design adds them. The redesign also removes the frequent-full-scan and wide-transaction findings the source shows. 7 keys have no cardinality statistics.
risks.mitigation: Give each of these queries the keys routing assumed in the DynamoDB design, check a key with few or unknown distinct values for hot partitions, and serve none of them as a scan. See the Wave 3 gate in the roadmap.
details: A key on reviewable_claimed_topics.user_id: read as key-scoped 1:N read instead of ad hoc filter. With a key on reviewable_claimed_topics.user_id the write is key scoped (changes the rows one user_id value of reviewable_claimed_topics addresses, a key that is not unique: a key-scoped multi-item write (a Query plus a batch write)): one Query on that key and a batch write.
A whole read of a small reference table, which the design keeps as one item collection or caches.

Keys on category_custom_fields.name, directory_columns.name, email_tokens.email, push_subscriptions.user_id, theme_settings.theme_id and topic_embeds.topic_id: each read as key-scoped 1:N read instead of ad hoc filter.

risks.description: [dynamodb] DynamoDB serves 13 statements on 10 tables poorly (scores 11 to 26, below 50): retention delete (6), consistency repair sweep (3), orphan clean-up (2), delete by any of several references (1) and duplicate clean-up (1). A table has one writer, so each moves with the other statements that write its table.
risks.mitigation: Design these statements in DynamoDB for what they are for, the target's own way, not as a copy of the source's set-based SQL; each statement's detail names the approach. See the Wave 3 gate in the roadmap.

mitigation_strategies: Load-test the queries behind RISK-004 on Aurora PostgreSQL with production-scale data before cutover.
Apply the mitigations of RISK-001, RISK-002 and RISK-003.

After wave 1 (Aurora PostgreSQL): compare the latency of 1654 queries with their source baseline (weighted average 0.06 ms) and check the engine sustains the design rate of 39.1 requests/s before starting wave 2.
After wave 2 (ElastiCache): track the cache hit rate for the 3 hot reads it fronts on Aurora PostgreSQL (25.1% of calls, 9.8 calls/s) and compare their latency with the source before starting wave 3.
After wave 3 (DynamoDB and DocumentDB): compare the latency of 858 queries with their source baseline (weighted average 0.04 ms) and check the engine sustains the design rate of 25 requests/s.

resolved_risks.description: [aurora_postgresql] Kept on Aurora PostgreSQL because of multi-table joins on this table.
resolved_risks.reason: Aurora PostgreSQL is also required for multi-table joins on this table, so keeping it there is a deliberate routing decision, not an open risk; revisit DynamoDB for this table's simple key-value reads in a later wave if those other queries are retired or move too

resolved_risks.description: [aurora_postgresql] Moved to DocumentDB: Table with no foreign keys and no join participation: all queries are single-table CRUD. Aurora serves single-table CRUD natively and uses none of its relational features for it (Amazon Aurora User Guide, What is Amazon Aurora).
resolved_risks.reason: the queries moved to DocumentDB, whose schema design serves all of them

resolved_risks.description: [aurora_postgresql] Moved to DynamoDB: Table with no foreign keys and no join participation: all queries are single-table CRUD. Aurora serves single-table CRUD natively and uses none of its relational features for it (Amazon Aurora User Guide, What is Amazon Aurora).
resolved_risks.reason: the Aurora PostgreSQL analysis recommended DynamoDB for these queries and the assignment moved them there

resolved_risks.description: [aurora_postgresql] Moved to DocumentDB: Table accessed by at most 2 distinct query patterns, all single-table, all by primary key or single column filter. Aurora serves these reads natively and its query optimizer adds nothing to them (Amazon Aurora User Guide, What is Amazon Aurora).
resolved_risks.reason: the queries moved to DocumentDB, whose schema design serves all of them

resolved_risks.description: [documentdb] Queries joining 3 or more tables. Each join becomes a $lookup stage that reads the joined collection for the documents flowing through it, one stage per collection, with a nested-loop, hash or sort-merge algorithm (Amazon DocumentDB Developer Guide, Functional differences, $lookup); correlated $lookup needs DocumentDB 8.0.2 or later.
resolved_risks.reason: the queries run as SQL on Aurora PostgreSQL

resolved_risks.description: [documentdb] Queries with NOT IN, <>, !=, NOT EXISTS, which map to $ne/$nin/$nor. Query planner version 2 and later use indexes for $ne, $nin and $not, so a negation is no worse on DocumentDB than on an engine where it is rarely index-selective (Amazon DocumentDB Developer Guide, Query planner).
resolved_risks.reason: the queries run as SQL on Aurora PostgreSQL

resolved_risks.description: [documentdb] SQL window functions $setWindowFields serves (ROW_NUMBER, RANK, running totals): DocumentDB 8.0.2 or later on an instance-based cluster. LAG and LEAD ($shift) and NTILE (no bucketing window operator) run on no version, so they are a hard capability gap, not this entry (Amazon DocumentDB Developer Guide, Supported MongoDB APIs, operations, and data types).
resolved_risks.reason: the queries run as SQL on Aurora PostgreSQL

resolved_risks.description: [documentdb] Queries with correlated subqueries. A correlated $lookup (let/pipeline) runs its sub-pipeline for each input document, and needs DocumentDB 8.0.2 or later on an instance-based cluster (Amazon DocumentDB Developer Guide, Supported MongoDB APIs, operations, and data types); otherwise pre-denormalize.
resolved_risks.reason: the queries run as SQL on Aurora PostgreSQL

resolved_risks.description: [documentdb] Moved to DynamoDB: Queries with correlated subqueries. A correlated $lookup (let/pipeline) runs its sub-pipeline for each input document, and needs DocumentDB 8.0.2 or later on an instance-based cluster (Amazon DocumentDB Developer Guide, Supported MongoDB APIs, operations, and data types); otherwise pre-denormalize.
resolved_risks.reason: the queries moved to DynamoDB, whose schema design serves all of them

resolved_risks.description: [documentdb] Self-referential FKs or recursive queries. $graphLookup runs on DocumentDB 8.0 instance-based clusters, not on 5.0 or earlier and not on elastic clusters (Amazon DocumentDB Developer Guide, Supported MongoDB APIs, operations, and data types).
resolved_risks.reason: the queries run as SQL on Aurora PostgreSQL

resolved_risks.description: [dynamodb] The first rows of a whole table in some order (ORDER BY with a row limit and no key value). A DynamoDB Scan returns items in no particular order, so the first rows by any order need every item read and sorted by the application (Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide, Scanning tables).
resolved_risks.reason: the queries run as SQL on Aurora PostgreSQL

resolved_risks.description: [dynamodb] Moved to DocumentDB: The first rows of a whole table in some order (ORDER BY with a row limit and no key value). A DynamoDB Scan returns items in no particular order, so the first rows by any order need every item read and sorted by the application (Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide, Scanning tables).
resolved_risks.reason: the queries moved to DocumentDB, whose schema design serves all of them

resolved_risks.description: [dynamodb] GROUP BY, HAVING, or an aggregate over rows no key anchors or over a join (one key's COUNT or SUM is a Query on that key, not this pattern). DynamoDB has no server-side aggregation: a Query or Scan can only count the items it reads (Select = COUNT), so a grouped result needs the application layer, pre-computed aggregates or a separate analytics store (Amazon DynamoDB API Reference, Query).
resolved_risks.reason: the queries run as SQL on Aurora PostgreSQL

resolved_risks.description: [dynamodb] A write wider than one transaction: more than 100 items, or rows a range, join, subquery or a filter with no key anchor picks (a write by a non-unique key column is a key-scoped Query plus batch write, not this). DynamoDB TransactWriteItems holds up to 100 items and 4 MB across tables (Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide, Amazon DynamoDB Transactions).
resolved_risks.reason: the schema design covers every flagged query
